outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the bounds 9 ≤ max χ(biplanar) ≤ 12 have not moved; the one in-window event bearing on the problem is a single-author arXiv preprint dated 23 September 2026 (Szeider, arXiv:2609.28102) proving every biplanar graph with independence number at most 2 is 9-colourable, which restricts but does not settle the maximum.
problem_asks: The maximum chromatic number over all biplanar graphs (graphs whose edge set can be split into two planar graphs on the same vertex set, i.e. thickness at most 2). Parts: (a) the exact value of that maximum, an integer; (b) the lower end, a biplanar graph attaining the maximum; (c) the upper end, a proof that every biplanar graph is that many-colourable. Status before 2024: lower end 9 (Sulanke), upper end 12 (Ringel, by a degeneracy count). Open: whether the value is 9, 10, 11 or 12. Gethner conjectured 11 (2018). Whether every biplanar graph is 11-colourable is also open.

events.what_happened: Gerhard Ringel posed the problem in 1959 as an extension of the map-colouring problem (Earth countries with Moon colonies that share a colour). Epoch AI, Wikipedia's lead, and search summaries credit Ringel with proving every biplanar graph is 12-colourable. Wikipedia's article (as fetched through a summariser) says Ringel showed the answer lies between 8 and 12 and conjectured 8, citing Gardner 1980 for the conjecture. The original 1959 text was not located or opened, and its venue is unverified.
events.revisions: Venue and month not located. The 1965 date that appeared in one of my own query strings is not supported by any source found.
events.delivers: Upper end: every biplanar graph is 12-colourable (χ ≤ 12). Also the conjecture that the maximum is 8, which the Sulanke 9-chromatic example refuted.
events.remains: The exact maximum within {9, 10, 11, 12}; both the lower end above 9 and the upper end below 12.
events.directly_checkable: The 12-bound is a short count. A biplanar graph on n ≥ 3 vertices has at most 2(3n−6) = 6n−12 edges, so its average degree is below 12 and some vertex has degree at most 11. Repeatedly deleting such a vertex and colouring in reverse order uses at most 12 colours. Checkable by hand, and set out in the Barbados 2018 list and the Open Problem Garden entry.
events.direction: Upper-end bound: the maximum is at most 12. Does not cut against any assertion in the statement. The 8-conjecture cut against the lower end and was refuted.

events.what_happened: J. Hutchinson, 'Coloring Ordinary Maps, Maps of Empires, and Maps of the Moon', Mathematics Magazine 66(4), pp. 211–226 (October 1993). Wikipedia, as fetched through a summariser, cites it for the degeneracy argument giving χ ≤ 12. Not opened; expository article, so it is recorded as a source of the attribution dispute rather than as a result.
events.delivers: Expository. As far as the secondary sources show, it restates the 12-bound via degeneracy and the map formulations. No new bound identified. Not verified against the article.
events.direction: Restates the upper end (12). No cut.

events.what_happened: Thom Sulanke's example: the join C5 ∨ K6 of a 5-cycle with a complete graph on 6 vertices (11 vertices in total) is biplanar and has chromatic number 9, since χ(join) = χ(C5) + χ(K6) = 3 + 6. This refuted Ringel's conjecture of 8. The first public written account I located is Martin Gardner's Scientific American column 'Mathematical Recreations: The Coloring of Unusual Maps Leads Into Uncharted Territory' (February 1980), as cited by MathWorld (search summary). The discovery date is disputed (see disputes). Primary sources were not opened.
events.revisions: The discovery date is disputed: 1973 (Bridges 2024 artist biography; a search summary of arXiv:2609.28102, not confirmed in its text), 1974 (Wikipedia; a UCI article; a 2023 Graph Drawing talk), 1975 (a Leiden student thesis, which says Sulanke found it in response to a March 1975 Gardner column and wrote to Gardner), 1980 (Epoch AI; the Gardner column). The Gardner column is a magazine article, not a journal of record.
events.delivers: Lower end: a biplanar graph with χ = 9, so the maximum is at least 9. Refutes the conjectured maximum of 8.
events.remains: Whether the maximum is 9, or is 10, 11 or 12. The question of a biplanar graph with χ ≥ 10 stays open.
events.directly_checkable: Yes. The join has 11 vertices, and χ = 9 follows from χ(G ∨ H) = χ(G) + χ(H). Biplanarity needs an explicit split of its edges into two planar graphs. The Wolfram Demonstrations page describes such a split as two planar 11-region maps sharing 50 of 55 possible borders. I did not check that split myself.
events.doubts: None substantive about the chromatic number of 9. The biplanarity of the join rests on a decomposition the secondary sources describe and I did not check.
events.direction: Lower end: a 9-chromatic biplanar graph. It cuts against the conjectured value 8 and supports the lower bound 9.
events.object: The join C5 ∨ K6: a 5-cycle with every vertex joined to every vertex of a K6, on 11 vertices. It is biplanar (its edges split into two planar graphs on the same 11 vertices) and has χ = 9. This is an explicit graph, not an existence proof. The split is described in secondary sources and was not checked by me.

events.what_happened: Adilov (2018), cited in a search summary of arXiv:2609.28102 as giving, for biplanar graphs with girth at least 10, chromatic number at most 5. Not opened, and I could not find the primary source, so the date is only the year cited.
events.delivers: A restricted class (girth at least 10) with χ ≤ 5. Says nothing about the maximum over all biplanar graphs.
events.remains: The whole problem; this is a restricted class.
events.doubts: Known only from a secondary mention; the primary source is not identified.
events.direction: Restricted-class upper bound on a different quantity. No cut against the statement.

events.what_happened: D. L. Boutin, E. Gethner and T. Sulanke, 'Thickness-two graphs part one: new nine-critical graphs, permuted layer graphs, and Catlin's graphs', Journal of Graph Theory 57(3):198–214 (2008). Per secondary summaries (the Szeider 2026 introduction, and a Wikipedia reference list), they constructed further 9-critical biplanar graphs on 12 to 16 vertices. Not opened.
events.revisions: Earlier arXiv or preprint posting not checked.
events.delivers: Lower end: further biplanar 9-critical graphs, so further witnesses that the maximum is at least 9. Does not change the bounds.
events.direction: Lower end; more witnesses at 9. No cut against any assertion.
events.object: Further 9-critical biplanar graphs on 12 to 16 vertices, by the families named in the title. Named only; not opened.

events.what_happened: E. Gethner and T. Sulanke, 'Thickness-two graphs Part Two', Graphs and Combinatorics 25(2):197–217 (2009), per a search summary. Per the Szeider 2026 introduction, they found eight 9-critical biplanar graphs on 17 vertices with triangle-free complement (independence number 2), and posed Open Problem 1(a): find a thickness-two graph on 19 vertices with triangle-free complement. Not opened.
events.delivers: Lower end: further 9-critical biplanar graphs with independence number 2. Poses the 19-vertex question, since such a graph would have χ ≥ 10. Does not move any bound.
events.remains: The whole maximum. The 19-vertex question was answered negatively in 2026 (see the Szeider event), but only in the independence-number-2 class.
events.direction: Lower end; poses an open question that a later event answered negatively.
events.object: Eight 9-critical biplanar graphs on 17 vertices with triangle-free complement, per secondary summary. Not opened.

events.what_happened: P. Ossona de Mendez, S. Oum and D. Wood, 'Defective colouring of graphs excluding a subgraph or minor', arXiv:1611.09060 (November 2016). Per the 2018 Barbados list (quoted in search results), they proved every biplanar graph is 11-colourable with defect 2, meaning each colour class induces maximum degree 2. Not opened.
events.delivers: A defective-colouring result: every biplanar graph is 11-colourable with defect 2. This answers a different question, a defective rather than a proper colouring. It does not decide whether a proper 11-colouring exists.
events.remains: The whole problem; this is a variant.
events.direction: Defective-colouring variant; no cut against the proper maximum.

events.what_happened: K. Hendrey and D. Wood, 'Defective and Clustered Choosability of Sparse Graphs', arXiv:1806.07040 (June 2018; later Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 2019). Per the Barbados list, they showed Conjecture 1 (biplanar graphs are 11-colourable with bounded clustering) is true with clustering 9. Abstract seen in a search summary; not opened.
events.delivers: A clustered-colouring variant: biplanar graphs admit bounded-clustering colourings with few colours, including the clustering-9 statement attributed on the Barbados list. This is a clustered question, not the proper chromatic number.
events.doubts: The clustering-9 biplanar statement is credited to the Barbados update rather than to a statement I confirmed in the paper.
events.direction: Clustered variant; no cut against the proper maximum.

events.what_happened: 'Open Problems for the Barbados Graph Theory Workshop 2018' (Princeton). Problem 2 (D. Wood) and Problem 4 (D. Král') state the answer lies in 9 to 12, derive the upper bound from Euler's formula (11-degenerate, 12-colourable), record that it is unknown whether every biplanar graph is 11-colourable, and list Conjecture 1 (11-colourable with bounded clustering) with updates. The updates are: Hendrey and Wood, clustering 9; Hendrey, 9-coloured with clustering 2; Hendrey, 8-coloured with bounded clustering. The page as fetched gives no dates for these updates. Problem 4 also asks for an independent-set bound (c > 1/12) for biplanar graphs, which is a different question.
events.revisions: The list is dated 2018, but the update dates are not shown on the page as fetched. Some updates may postdate 26 January 2024. This is not established.
events.delivers: Restates the bounds 9 and 12 and records clustered and defective variants with updates. It is not a new result on the proper maximum.
events.remains: The exact maximum; whether every biplanar graph is 11-colourable; the clustered Conjecture 1 as updated.
events.direction: Restates the status quo: 9 ≤ max ≤ 12. No cut.

events.what_happened: E. Gethner, 'To the Moon and Beyond', chapter 10 of Graph Theory: Favorite Conjectures and Open Problems 2 (eds. Gera, Haynes, Hedetniemi; Springer, 2018). Per secondary summaries, she conjectures the answer is 11, offers candidate 10-chromatic biplanar graphs (including the strong product of a cycle with a clique, and a graph from deleting a vertex from another), and conjectures that 2-blowups of planar graphs are biplanar (refuted by Eppstein in 2023). The chapter text was not accessed.
events.delivers: Conjectures only: the maximum is conjectured to be 11, and candidate 10-chromatic graphs are offered. Biplanarity of the candidates is not established. No proof.
events.doubts: The conjecture of 11 has no supporting proof in any source. The candidate biplanarity is unresolved in the sources. One candidate (C5 ⊠ K4 minus a vertex) is reported as not biplanar in the 2023 SAT-based event below.
events.direction: Conjectures the maximum is 11 and proposes candidate constructions for values of 10 or more. Consistent with the open upper end.

events.what_happened: M. Kirchweger, M. Scheucher and S. Szeider, 'SAT-Based Generation of Planar Graphs', SAT 2023 (LIPIcs vol. 271, 14:1–14:18). The main subject is SAT-based generation of planar graphs with dynamic symmetry breaking. The table of contents includes an experiment section 5.2 'The Earth-Moon Problem'. Per Wikipedia (as fetched through a summariser), the paper confirmed that C5 ⊠ K4 minus a vertex, one of Gethner's candidates for χ = 10, is not biplanar. I could not read the PDF body, so the non-biplanarity claim and the Earth-Moon experiment's content are unverified.
events.delivers: Per Wikipedia: one candidate for χ ≥ 10 (C5 ⊠ K4 minus a vertex) is not biplanar, established by SAT computation. Closes one candidate route to a 10-chromatic example. Does not move any bound on the maximum.

checked_by.who: SAT 2023 programme committee and LIPIcs (peer-reviewed conference)
checked_by.qualification: A refereed venue for a SAT-based combinatorics paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed conference publication. I did not verify the referee process or read the paper body.

events.doubts: Only the table of contents and the Wikipedia summary were read. The claim about the candidate graph is unverified in the paper text.
events.direction: Cuts against one candidate route to a 10-chromatic biplanar graph (the candidate is not biplanar). No cut against the statement itself.

events.what_happened: D. Eppstein, 'On the Biplanarity of Blowups', arXiv:2301.09246 (v1 23 January 2023; v2 1 September 2023). Also GD 2023 (best paper award) and Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications 28(2):83–99 (2024). It disproves Gethner's conjecture that 2-blowups of planar graphs are biplanar, using iterated Kleetopes as counterexamples, and gives biplanar drawings for other 2-blowup classes. The abstract page does not mention the Earth-Moon problem.
events.revisions: v2 1 September 2023; journal version JGAA 28(2), 2024, pp. 83–99.
events.delivers: Restricted to 2-blowups of planar graphs: not all are biplanar (iterated Kleetopes are counterexamples). A question about biplanarity of a family, not about the chromatic number, so it does not change the maximum or its bounds.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed conference and journal publication, with a best-paper award at GD 2023
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for refereed publication and recognised with the GD 2023 best-paper award for combinatorial and algorithmic aspects

events.direction: A neighbouring question. Refutes a conjecture from Gethner's survey about blowups, not a claim about the chromatic number. It cuts against that conjecture, not against any assertion in the statement.
events.object: Iterated Kleetope-based 2-blowups: these are not biplanar and do not have split thickness two (a non-existence result). They are not objects for the maximum.

events.what_happened: S. Kitano, 'Upper Bounds of the Odd Chromatic Number of a Graph in terms of its Thickness', arXiv:2403.11555 (submitted 18 March 2024, one version). Per the abstract sentence quoted by my fetch: a graph with minimum degree at least 2θ(G)−1 and girth at least 6 is odd 6θ(G)-colourable, where θ is thickness. For thickness 2 that gives odd 12-colourability under minimum degree 3 and girth 6. The paper does not mention biplanar graphs or the Earth-Moon problem. A Japanese-language slide deck (kitano_sota.pdf, 2024) was listed in searches; its body was unreadable.
events.delivers: Odd chromatic number, a different parameter, for graphs of thickness θ. For thickness 2, odd-12-colourability under extra conditions. It says nothing about the ordinary chromatic number of biplanar graphs.
events.direction: Analogue (odd chromatic number), with restrictions. No cut against the proper maximum.

events.what_happened: A readthedocs page titled 'Biplanar (Thickness-2) Graph Chromatic Number' (mlehaptics). It says the page is the output of an automated cascade dispatched 2026-05-23 and cites Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems. It states the problem is open, gives χ ≥ 8 from K8 (biplanar, citing Beineke and Harary 1965), gives χ ≤ 11 by a 'standard degeneracy argument' ('each planar graph is 5-degenerate; union of two is at most 10-degenerate') with no source, and says most researchers believe χ ≤ 9. It does not mention Sulanke's 9-chromatic graph.
events.delivers: Claims χ ≤ 11. The argument as stated does not establish that: the step from two 5-degenerate graphs to a 10-degenerate union is unsupported, and the standard edge count gives 11-degenerate and so 12 colours. Its lower bound of 8 is weaker than the known 9. No new bound established.
events.doubts: The page ignores Sulanke's 9-chromatic graph while giving χ ≥ 8 and asserting that most researchers believe χ ≤ 9. Its upper-end argument does not follow from the facts it states. Its references (Beineke and Harary 1965; Hoffman 1970) are flagged by the page as unverified. It is a machine-generated 'cascade', and the page does not say who or what wrote the text.
events.direction: Asserts a bound (χ ≤ 11) that would cut the upper end, but the argument does not support it. No cut established.

events.what_happened: Stefan Szeider (TU Wien; sole author), 'Biplanar graphs with independence number two are 9-colorable', arXiv:2609.28102, v1 submitted 23 September 2026. Abstract and introduction state that the largest chromatic number of a biplanar graph is known to lie between 9 and 12, and that Gethner and Sulanke asked in 2009 whether a 19-vertex biplanar graph with independence number 2 exists. Theorem 1: every biplanar graph with independence number at most 2 is 9-colourable. Theorem 2: no biplanar graph on 19 vertices has independence number at most 2. The method embeds a hypothetical counterexample in the union of two sphere triangulations, enumerates 3271 candidate complements with SAT modulo symmetries (checked against geng), refutes each with CaDiCaL, handles the 18-vertex universal-vertex case separately, and reduces the general case by a matching / Gallai–Edmonds argument. The computational part is checked in Lean 4, per the abstract. A Zenodo record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22913639; 'Lean development, certificates, and reproduction instructions', published 23 September 2026, v1) holds the Lean development (Lean v4.30.0, Mathlib v4.30.0), the SAT instances and certificates.
events.revisions: v1 only (23 September 2026) as of 11 October 2026; no v2 listed on the arXiv abstract page fetched that day.
events.delivers: Restricted to biplanar graphs with independence number at most 2: all are 9-colourable (Theorem 1). Also no biplanar graph on 19 vertices has independence number at most 2 (Theorem 2), which answers the 2009 Gethner–Sulanke question. The result therefore rules out a 10-chromatic biplanar graph of independence number at most 2. It is restricted to that class and to the planarity hypotheses listed under doubts.
events.remains: The maximum: whether a biplanar graph with independence number at least 3 has χ ≥ 10; whether every biplanar graph is 9-colourable; the upper end (10 to 12) and Gethner's conjectured 11. The bounds 9 and 12 are unchanged.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (v4.30.0) with Mathlib v4.30.0; SAT certificates checked by an LRAT reader

events.directly_checkable: The 19-vertex question is concrete, but the proof's core is an enumeration of 3271 SAT-generated complements and their refutations. A reader can check the reduction by hand, but not the enumeration without the Zenodo artifacts.
events.doubts: Scope and trust caveats, not reasons to think the proof wrong. (1) The Lean results depend on three planarity facts stated as hypotheses: X1, subgraphs and induced subgraphs of planar graphs are planar; X2, for n ≥ 4 every planar graph on n vertices is a spanning subgraph of a planar sphere triangulation; X3, K9 is not biplanar (cited to Battle–Harary–Kodama, Biniaz, Tutte). The paper says planarity itself is not formalised. (2) The trust base includes the Lean kernel, compiler and runtime via native_decide, which the paper says introduces 6554 axioms, plus the LRAT-catcher reader; CaDiCaL, SMS and geng are not trusted but their outputs are checked. (3) The paper does not say whether sorry remains. (4) Single author, arXiv preprint, no journal, referee report or public expert reading found in 18 days. (5) The author states AI assistance was used for implementing the computation (see the ai block); the computation is the proof's core.
events.direction: Cuts against the existence of a biplanar graph with χ ≥ 10 whose independence number is at most 2. This does not contradict any assertion in the statement, and it does not decide whether a 10-chromatic biplanar graph with larger independence number exists.

disputes.summary: The date of Sulanke's 9-chromatic construction differs by source: 1973 (Bridges 2024 artist biography; a search summary of arXiv:2609.28102, not confirmed in its text), 1974 (Wikipedia; a UCI news item; a 2023 Graph Drawing talk), 1975 (a Leiden student thesis, which ties Sulanke's finding to a March 1975 Gardner column and a letter to Gardner), and 1980 (Epoch AI; Gardner's February 1980 Scientific American column, as cited by MathWorld). Not resolved. The record dates the event to 1980 because that is the earliest public written account I located.

The upper bound of 12 is credited to Ringel (1959) by Epoch AI, Wikipedia's lead, and search summaries, but Wikipedia attributes the degeneracy argument specifically to Hutchinson (1993). The 2018 Barbados list gives the Euler-formula argument without attribution. Not resolved.
Ringel's conjectured value of 8 is attributed to Ringel by some sources but cited to Gardner (1980) by Wikipedia. Not resolved.

The 9-colouring with clustering 2 is credited to Kopreski and Yu in a Hendrey–Wood survey (as reported in a search summary, the Kopreski–Yu paper not located) and to Hendrey in an update on the Barbados list. Not resolved.

Wikipedia credits the 2023 non-biplanarity result for the candidate C5 ⊠ K4 minus a vertex to Kirchweger, Scheucher and Szeider (2023). I could not read the paper body to confirm the claim or identify which candidate it covers. Not resolved.

summary: Searches found no change to the bounds 9 ≤ max χ(biplanar) ≤ 12 since 26 January 2024. The one in-window event bearing on the problem is Stefan Szeider's single-author arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.28102 (v1, 23 September 2026), which proves that every biplanar graph with independence number at most 2 is 9-colourable, and that no biplanar graph on 19 vertices has independence number at most 2, answering Gethner and Sulanke's 2009 question. I read the arXiv abstract and HTML rendering, and the Zenodo record; the PDF body could not be decoded. The result does not change any bound. It rules out one route to a 10-chromatic example, since Sulanke's graph and the 9-critical families have independence number 2, but the general maximum is still bracketed by 9 and 12. No peer review, journal decision, or public expert reading was found in the 18 days since posting. The authors' acknowledgements say: 'The author used AI assistance for implementing the computation, drafting the text, and adversarial review,' and that the author 'takes full responsibility for the content.' No system is named in the sources, so ai.systems is empty. I set none_found to false, because AI assistance is disclosed even though no system is named. Whether that assistance is load-bearing is a close call. The 3271-candidate enumeration, the SAT refutations and the Lean checks form the proof's computational core, and the AI helped implement them. The reduction and the 18-vertex case are the author's own work. Both readings are left for the later pass. The Lean development (Lean v4.30.0, Mathlib v4.30.0) assumes three planarity facts as hypotheses, and the paper says planarity itself is not formalised. The paper does not state whether sorry remains. Earlier events: Ringel's 12-bound (1959, attributed variously, see disputes); Sulanke's 9-chromatic join C5 ∨ K6 (discovery date disputed, first written account 1980); further 9-critical families (2008, 2009); defective and clustered variants (2016, 2018) and the 2018 Barbados list; Gethner's 2018 conjectures (maximum 11, candidate 10-chromatic graphs); a 2023 SAT result reported by Wikipedia as showing one candidate is not biplanar; Eppstein's 2023 refutation of Gethner's blowup conjecture, a neighbouring question; and a 2024 odd-chromatic analogue by Kitano. A May 2026 readthedocs page asserts χ ≤ 11 by an argument that does not establish it, and is recorded as discounted. Epoch AI's FrontierMath: Open Problems page lists a construction of a biplanar graph with χ ≥ 10 as an open AI-benchmark task, unsolved on the page. The page is a task, not a result, and I found no AI attempt reported. Opper AI roundtable pages were not relied on, as they are model opinion.
competing_reading: Read the Szeider result as a partial resolution. The statement asks for the maximum, and the result shows that any biplanar graph with χ ≥ 10 must have independence number at least 3. This removes the only known lower-bound family from consideration for a 10-chromatic example, so the problem could be counted as partly settled in a restricted class. The opposite reading: the result changes no quantity named in the statement, since the maximum is still bracketed by 9 and 12, so it is a restricted-class result that moves nothing. On AI: the disclosed assistance could be read as load-bearing, because it wrote the code that produces the enumeration and refutations on which Theorem 1 rests. Or it could be read as implementation support around mathematics the author supplied, namely the reduction to the 3271-graph computation and the 18-vertex case.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The arXiv TeX source or PDF body of 2609.28102: the exact acknowledgement sentence, whether any tool is named (for example in the Zenodo README or commit history), and which parts of the reduction were done by hand. (2) The Zenodo Lean files: whether any sorry remains, and what native_decide and the 6554 axioms cover. (3) The statements of X1 to X3 as written in the paper's Section 2, and whether X3 (K9 non-biplanar) is accepted as classical. (4) A referee report, journal acceptance, or a public expert reading. (5) Any later paper that treats biplanar graphs with independence number at least 3 and χ ≥ 10, or that proves every biplanar graph 11-colourable. (6) The dates of the Barbados updates, and the Kopreski–Yu paper, which would settle the clustering-2 attribution. (7) The primary Sulanke source, which would settle the 1973/1974/1975/1980 dispute. (8) The PDF body of SAT 2023 (LIPIcs 14), to confirm the C5 ⊠ K4 minus a vertex non-biplanarity claim.

event.what_happened: Stefan Szeider (TU Wien; sole author), 'Biplanar graphs with independence number two are 9-colorable', arXiv:2609.28102, v1 submitted 23 September 2026. Abstract and introduction state that the largest chromatic number of a biplanar graph is known to lie between 9 and 12, and that Gethner and Sulanke asked in 2009 whether a 19-vertex biplanar graph with independence number 2 exists. Theorem 1: every biplanar graph with independence number at most 2 is 9-colourable. Theorem 2: no biplanar graph on 19 vertices has independence number at most 2. The method embeds a hypothetical counterexample in the union of two sphere triangulations, enumerates 3271 candidate complements with SAT modulo symmetries (checked against geng), refutes each with CaDiCaL, handles the 18-vertex universal-vertex case separately, and reduces the general case by a matching / Gallai–Edmonds argument. The computational part is checked in Lean 4, per the abstract. A Zenodo record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22913639; 'Lean development, certificates, and reproduction instructions', published 23 September 2026, v1) holds the Lean development (Lean v4.30.0, Mathlib v4.30.0), the SAT instances and certificates.
event.revisions: v1 only (23 September 2026) as of 11 October 2026; no v2 listed on the arXiv abstract page fetched that day.
event.delivers: Restricted to biplanar graphs with independence number at most 2: all are 9-colourable (Theorem 1). Also no biplanar graph on 19 vertices has independence number at most 2 (Theorem 2), which answers the 2009 Gethner–Sulanke question. The result therefore rules out a 10-chromatic biplanar graph of independence number at most 2. It is restricted to that class and to the planarity hypotheses listed under doubts.
event.remains: The maximum: whether a biplanar graph with independence number at least 3 has χ ≥ 10; whether every biplanar graph is 9-colourable; the upper end (10 to 12) and Gethner's conjectured 11. The bounds 9 and 12 are unchanged.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (v4.30.0) with Mathlib v4.30.0; SAT certificates checked by an LRAT reader

event.directly_checkable: The 19-vertex question is concrete, but the proof's core is an enumeration of 3271 SAT-generated complements and their refutations. A reader can check the reduction by hand, but not the enumeration without the Zenodo artifacts.
event.doubts: Scope and trust caveats, not reasons to think the proof wrong. (1) The Lean results depend on three planarity facts stated as hypotheses: X1, subgraphs and induced subgraphs of planar graphs are planar; X2, for n ≥ 4 every planar graph on n vertices is a spanning subgraph of a planar sphere triangulation; X3, K9 is not biplanar (cited to Battle–Harary–Kodama, Biniaz, Tutte). The paper says planarity itself is not formalised. (2) The trust base includes the Lean kernel, compiler and runtime via native_decide, which the paper says introduces 6554 axioms, plus the LRAT-catcher reader; CaDiCaL, SMS and geng are not trusted but their outputs are checked. (3) The paper does not say whether sorry remains. (4) Single author, arXiv preprint, no journal, referee report or public expert reading found in 18 days. (5) The author states AI assistance was used for implementing the computation (see the ai block); the computation is the proof's core.
event.direction: Cuts against the existence of a biplanar graph with χ ≥ 10 whose independence number is at most 2. This does not contradict any assertion in the statement, and it does not decide whether a 10-chromatic biplanar graph with larger independence number exists.

events.credibility_reason: Known only from a secondary mention; primary source not identified.

Its chi <= 11 argument rests on an unsupported key step (two 5-degenerate graphs giving a 10-degenerate union); the edge count gives only 11-degeneracy, so 12 colours. It also ignores the known 9-chromatic example.

judgement.why: The bounds 9 <= max <= 12 are unchanged since the snapshot. Szeider 2026 is scored `case`: within the class of biplanar graphs with independence number at most 2, it shows every graph is 9-colourable, and Sulanke's 9-chromatic join (independence number 2) sits in that class, so the maximum for that restriction is now determined. That makes it a settled restriction, not just an approach. The alternative was `none`, since no bound on the full maximum moved. It is unreviewed (preprint, 18 days old, Lean check only with planarity facts taken as hypotheses) but credible. On AI: ai.systems is empty with none_found false, so the role is `none`. The disclosure ('AI assistance for implementing the computation, drafting the text, and adversarial review') credits no named system with mathematics in the result: implementing a computation the author designed is implementation, not a contribution to the argument. Direction is `confirmed` because the result agrees with the class maximum being 9 and refutes nothing in the statement. Before the snapshot, Ringel's 12 and Sulanke's 9 are checkable bounds. The defective, clustered, odd-chromatic and blowup results answer different questions (variant). The surveys, further 9-critical families and the SAT check on one candidate move no bound (none). The 2026 readthedocs page is knocked down because its key step is wrong.
judgement.doubts: Szeider's scope is a close call between `case` and `none`; it rests on reading 'maximum chromatic number restricted to independence number <= 2' as a restriction of the question. The AI disclosure names no system, and the full acknowledgement was read only through a summariser. If the AI wrote code that generated the 3271-candidate enumeration, some might call that assisted; on the quote as given, it was implementation support. The Barbados update dates are unknown, and some updates may postdate the snapshot, but they are clustered variants in any case.
